podcast.title: Cameo in Singles (1992)
podcast.body: Chris Cornell made a cameo appearance in the 1992 Hollywood motion picture *Singles*. The film was significant for not only featuring the music of the moment but also including appearances from prominent bands and figures of the burgeoning alternative and grunge scene, helping to expand grunge's reach. "It was a Hollywood motion picture that not only featured the music of the moment, but also cameos from Pearl Jam and Chris Cornell and Allison Chains."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Singles (1992) – Walk-On Cameo and Spoonman Song Origin
podcast.body: Director Cameron Crowe cast Cornell in a brief, non-speaking walk-on role in *Singles* (1991, released 1992), appearing after a scene where Matt Dillon shows Bridget Fonda his new car stereo, immediately preceding a Soundgarden concert sequence. "Chris Cornell walks up to see what's going on. It doesn't say anything, but the very next shot is of Chris and Soundgarden on stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Soundgarden Breakup (1997) – Tension from Manager/Wife Susan Silver and Separate Tour Transport
podcast.body: The band broke up in 1997 partly due to the unresolvable conflict of interest created by Cornell being married to Susan Silver, who was also the band's manager (and the manager of Alice in Chains and Screaming Trees). By the end of the band's existence, each member was reportedly traveling separately by their own bus or plane between shows. After the divorce in 2002, Cornell filed a complaint with the California Labor Commission in 2006 alleging Silver had performed booking work without the required talent agent's license, and sought return of money she made from Soundgarden activities in 2005. "No conflict of interest there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lawsuit Against Ex-Wife Susan Silver (2004) – Royalties and Possessions Dispute
podcast.body: After divorcing Susan Silver in 2004, Chris Cornell sued her for a million dollars. He claimed she diverted Soundgarden royalties to the other band members and withheld valuable items, including a guitar, Grammy Awards, demo tapes, personal recordings, diaries, and journals. This legal dispute was cited as a reason for the prolonged delay in the Soundgarden reunion, although everything was eventually settled. "Chris sued Susan for a million dollars, claiming that she diverted Soundgarden royalties away from him and to the other three band members, words like fraud, oppression, and malice reused in the documents."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Stalker Death Threats (2004–) – Million-Dollar Security Overhaul, Threats to Kill Children
podcast.body: Beginning in 2004, when his wife Vicki was six months pregnant with their first child, Chris Cornell received a sustained campaign of threatening letters and emails containing explicit, detailed descriptions of how Vicki and their children — Toni (age 3) and Christopher Jr. (age 1) — would be killed. The writer or writers demonstrated knowledge of the family's address at their Beverly Hills mansion. Messages included lines such as "you stole my baby and now the baby must die." The Cornells spent over a million dollars on security: fences, more than 40 closed-circuit video cameras, alarms, and 24-hour guards. "They spent more than a million dollars on security, fences, more than 40 close circuit video cameras, alarms, 24-hour guards."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Audioslave Vocalist (Pre-2005)
podcast.body: He was the singer for Audioslave, which was formed from the members of Rage Against the Machine, contributing to the mid-2000s rock renaissance. "Chris Cornell of Soundguard doing the singing."

podcast.title: Black Calvarros Restaurant, Paris (2006) – Rock Music Bar Near the Four Seasons, Closed After Two Years
podcast.body: Cornell opened a high-end restaurant in Paris called Black Calvarros in 2006, located across from the Four Seasons hotel about five blocks from the Champs-Élysées. During renovations, a ceiling fresco dating to the 1780s was discovered. The joint venture with his wife Vicki and brother-in-law DJ Nick Blast offered food including caramelized quail, truffled mac and cheese, and gourmet hot dogs. Interior design was by the designer of the annual Victoria's Secret Fashion Show. The restaurant sometimes did not close until 7am but shut down after a couple of years. "A restaurant slash bar where you could go in Paris to hear rock music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grammy Nomination for "You Know My Name" (2006)
podcast.body: Chris Cornell's "You Know My Name" for the 2006 film "Casino Royale" was not only a critical success but also received a Grammy nomination. This recognition highlighted its quality and its successful integration into the Bond theme tradition. "The song was a critical success and it was even nominated for a Grammy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration for "You Know My Name" (2006)
podcast.body: While writing "You Know My Name" for "Casino Royale," Chris Cornell listened repeatedly to Tom Jones's "Thunderball" (1965) and Paul McCartney's "Live and Let Die" (1973) for inspiration. He aimed to create something new that still resonated with Bond tradition, leading to a critically acclaimed and Grammy-nominated song. "And one song that he listened to over and over again was Tom Jones's Thunderball a theme from 1965. He also listened to Live in Let Die a lot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Motorcycle Accident (October 24, 2006) – Hit by Truck, Thrown 20 Feet, $50,000 Bike Destroyed, Returned to Studio Same Day
podcast.body: While recording his second solo album, Cornell was riding his motorcycle through Studio City, Los Angeles, when he collided with a truck (reports conflict on whether it was a rear-end or front-end collision). He was thrown 20 feet into the air and his $50,000 bike was completely destroyed. Despite cuts and bruises, he dusted himself off and returned to the studio later the same day. "Given what could have happened to him."

podcast.title: Performance with Chester Bennington (2008)
podcast.body: During the 2008 Project Revolution Tour, Chris Cornell was performing when Chester Bennington unexpectedly joined him on stage to sing "Hunger Strike." This Temple of the Dog song was written by Cornell as a tribute to his late roommate, Andrew Wood of Mother Lovevont. "If we go back to the 2008 project revolution tour, Chris was on the bill. And when he stepped forward to sing the Temple of Dog Song, Hunger Strike, a song written for and dedicated to Chris's late roommate Andrew Wood of Mother Lovevont, Chester surprised everybody by coming in to sing with him."

podcast.title: Death (May 17–18, 2017) – MGM Grand Detroit, Ativan, Unknown Barbiturates, Naloxone Found in System
podcast.body: After a Soundgarden show at the MGM Grand in Detroit, Cornell returned to room 1136. His wife Vicki, 2,000 miles away in Los Angeles, noticed the house lights flickering via a remote app on Chris's phone and called him at 11:35pm — twenty minutes after he left the stage. His bodyguard Martin had given him two Ativan (lorazepam) tablets beforehand to help him sleep. Cornell told Vicki he was fine but sounded groggy and slurred. Martin was sent to check on him at 12:15am, found the room locked, kicked the door in, found the bathroom locked, kicked that door in, and found Chris on the floor with blood from his mouth and an exercise band around his neck. A hotel medic arrived at 12:56am; paramedics followed; Chris was pronounced dead at 1:30am. The official cause was suicide by hanging. Toxicology found Ativan, unknown barbiturates, and unexplained Nalozone (naloxone, an anti-opioid) in his system. A hidden injury was mentioned in two clinical reports but not in the autopsy. In 2018 Vicki sued Dr. Robert Coblin of Beverly Hills, who had prescribed the Ativan, alleging dangerous over-prescription to a known former addict; the lawsuit settled out of court in May 2021. "Many of us who know Chris well noticed that he wasn't himself during his final hours and that something was very off."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death (May 18, 2017) – Passing in Detroit
podcast.body: Chris Cornell passed away on May 18, 2017, in Detroit at the age of 52. His death marked the end of one of the pivotal figures whose bands made Grunge and Alt Rock possible, leaving behind a tremendous musical legacy. "On May 18th, 2017, Chris Cornell, singer for Soundgarden and audio slave, passed away in Detroit."

podcast.title: Death at MGM Grand (March 3, 2017)
podcast.body: Chris Cornell died by hanging himself in room 1136 of the MGM Grand in Detroit on March 3, 2017, after performing a gig at the Fox Theatre. After the show, he returned to the hotel with his bodyguard, Martin Christen, and was experiencing anxiety. He had taken some Ativan tablets and later told his wife, Vicki, in a phone call around 11:35 pm, that he had taken an "extra Ativan or two," slurring his words and sounding groggy. Vicki called Martin around 12:15 am, asking him to check on Chris. Martin found the room locked, and after hotel security refused assistance, he kicked in the door. He then kicked in the locked bathroom door, finding Chris on the floor with an exercise band around his neck and blood from his mouth. Paramedics were called at 12:56 am, CPR was performed, but he was pronounced dead at 1:30 am. "Chris Cornell, who died on March 3, 2017 in room 11.36 of the MGM Grand Hotel in Detroit."

podcast.title: Death by Suicide (May 18, 2017)
podcast.body: Chris Cornell was found dead by suicide in the early morning of May 18, 2017, at the MGM Grand Hotel in Detroit. His death occurred just a couple of hours after Soundgarden had performed a show at the Fox Theatre the night before. This event profoundly devastated his close friend, Chester Bennington. "The big shock was Chris Cornell's suicide. He was found dead early in the morning of May 18, 2017 in the MGM Grand Hotel in Detroit, just a couple of hours after the band played a show at the Fox Theatre the night before."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death by Suicide (May 18, 2017)
podcast.body: Chris Cornell died by suicide by hanging on May 18, 2017, at 1:30 AM, a death that came as a "real shock" to many. He was found in his hotel room (room 1136 at the MGM Grand, Detroit) with a red exercise band around his neck, attached to a carabiner jammed tightly into the doorframe. The night before, May 17, Soundgarden played a show at the Fox Theatre in Detroit, after which his long-time tour manager felt Chris was "messed up and struggling." Back at the hotel, his bodyguard, Martin Kirsten, gave him two Ativan pills, for which Chris had a prescription. Shortly after, Chris spoke to his wife Vicki, who noted his slurred speech; he claimed to have taken "too much Ativan" and was "just tired." He abruptly hung up, alarming Vicki. Martin Kirsten, called by Vicki, found Chris's room latched from the inside. After kicking open both the room and bathroom doors, he found Chris. The toxicology report found Ativan (four doses), pseudoephedrine, butylbital, caffeine, and Narcan (administered by paramedics). While his wife speculated drugs contributed to an "altered mental state," the police ruled it suicide by hanging. "Chris was pronounced dead at 1.30, and the police ruled a suicide by hanging."

podcast.title: Death in Detroit (2017)
podcast.body: Chris Cornell passed away on May 18, 2017, in room 1136 of the MGM Grand Hotel in Detroit. The tragedy occurred shortly after Soundgarden had performed at the nearby Fox Hotel. Feeling anxious after the show and fearing insomnia, Cornell took a couple of Ativan tablets. He spoke to his wife at 11:35 PM, then his bodyguard found him at 12:15 AM in a locked bathroom with a red exercise band around his neck and blood from his mouth after kicking in the door. He was declared dead at 1:30 AM, with the coroner ruling it suicide by hanging. His widow, Vicki Cornell, subsequently sued his doctor for prescribing Ativan. "At 130, Chris Cornell was declared dead. A coroner's report would rule that it was suicide, death by hanging."

podcast.title: Discovery of Death (2017)
podcast.body: Concerned by Chris's abrupt hang-up, Vicki called Martin Kirsten, who returned to room 1136 around 12:15 AM, approximately 40 minutes after his last departure. Despite having a key, the door was latched from the inside. Security refused to open it without authorization, so Kirsten kicked the door open. After searching the room and finding the bathroom door locked, he kicked that open as well. Inside, Cornell was found on the floor with blood around his mouth and a red exercise band around his neck, which was attached to a carabiner tightly jammed into the doorframe. Paramedics arrived just before 1 AM, but it was too late. Chris was pronounced dead at 1:30 AM, with police ruling it a suicide by hanging. "Inside, Cornell was found laying on the floor, blood running down his mouth and a red exercise band around his neck. The band had been attached to a carbonyl, which is a type of shackle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Events Leading to Discovery (Late May 17 - Early May 18, 2017)
podcast.body: After the Soundgarden show, Chris Cornell returned to his hotel room (1136 at the MGM Grand) with his bodyguard, Martin Kirsten. Kirsten helped with Cornell's laptop and gave him two prescribed Ativan pills before leaving at 11:35 PM. Soon after, Cornell spoke with his wife Vicki on the phone, his speech slurred, saying he "probably took too much Ativan" and was "just tired," before abruptly hanging up. Alarmed, Vicki called Kirsten, who returned to the room at 12:15 AM. Finding the door latched from the inside, Kirsten, after being denied entry by security, kicked open the door. He found the bathroom door also locked and kicked that open, discovering Cornell on the floor with blood from his mouth and a red exercise band around his neck, attached to a carabiner jammed into the doorframe. "Martin left Chris' room at around 11.35. Soon after that, Chris spoke with his wife Vicki on the phone. She says his speech was slurred."

podcast.title: Last Known Interactions (2017)
podcast.body: By 11:30 PM, Chris Cornell was back in his hotel room (1136) at the MGM Grand, about half a mile from the venue, accompanied by his bodyguard, Martin Kirsten. Chris asked Kirsten for help with his laptop, and during this time, Kirsten gave Chris two Ativan pills, for which Chris had a prescription for anti-anxiety medication. Kirsten left the room around 11:35 PM. Soon after, Chris spoke with his wife, Vicki, on the phone; she noted his speech was slurred and he repeatedly said he "probably took too much Ativan" and was "just tired," before abruptly hanging up. "His bodyguard, Martin Kirsten, was with him. Something was wrong with Chris' laptop and he wanted Martin to help him out with it. So as he looked at his computer, Martin gave Chris to out of Ann Pills."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Toxicology Report and Contributing Factors (Post-May 2017)
podcast.body: Chris Cornell's toxicology report revealed several substances in his system: four doses of Ativan (an anti-anxiety medication he had a prescription for), pseudoephedrine (a common over-the-counter decongestant), butylbital (a sedative and strong painkiller), caffeine (from No-Doz tablets), and Narcan (likely administered by paramedics, who might have initially suspected an opioid overdose). While some sources mentioned "barbiturates," this likely referred to butylbital, which is a barbiturate. Although broken ribs were found, they were likely caused by EMS during chest compressions. His wife suggested that the drugs might have contributed to an "altered mental state" that prompted his decision. "When the toxicology report came back, they found the out-of-end, four doses of it, which is a lot, but less than cases where out-of-end has been implicated in a death."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Toxicology Report and Speculation (2017)
podcast.body: The toxicology report found four doses of Ativan, pseudoephedrine (a common over-the-counter decongestant), butalbital (a sedative and strong painkiller), caffeine (likely from a No-Doz tablet), and Narcan (administered by paramedics for a suspected opioid overdose). Some sources also mentioned barbiturates, likely referring to butalbital. While broken ribs were noted, they were attributed to EMS chest compressions. Chris had no prior record of being suicidal, leading to speculation by his wife and others that the drugs may have induced an "altered mental state" that prompted a terrible, spur-of-the-moment decision. "When the toxicology report came back, they found the out-of-end, four doses of it, which is a lot, but less than cases where out-of-end has been implicated in a death."

podcast.title: Audioslave Manager Conflict – Near Breakup
podcast.body: The new group, which would become Audioslave, faced immediate challenges when their respective managers began brawling, causing the band to break up before playing their first gig. This administrative hurdle required both managers to be fired and a new management group to be brought in to resolve the issues. "Well, the new group broke up before they played their first gig because the two managers started brawling, and it looked like Rage Against the Machine version 2.0 was dead before it got a chance to do anything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Audition for Rage Against the Machine – Rick Rubin's Suggestion
podcast.body: After his solo album's disappointing sales, and with Rage Against the Machine's singer Zack de la Rocha having quit, producer Rick Rubin suggested Chris Cornell as a potential new vocalist for the remaining members. The chemistry between Cornell and the instrumentalists was instantaneous, leading them to write 21 songs in just 19 days. "Then producer Rick Rubin suggested that they ring up Chris Cornell. The chemistry was so instant that they wrote 21 songs in just 19 days."

podcast.body: Chris Cornell was a very close friend of Chester Bennington, and his death significantly impacted Bennington. "We can't talk about the death of Chris Cornell, without immediately going to Chester Bennington of Lincoln Park. He and Chris were great, great friends."

podcast.title: Close Relationship with Chester Bennington
podcast.body: Chris Cornell and Chester Bennington were described as "very, very close" and "kindred spirits." Cornell's death, which occurred on what would have been his 53rd birthday (the same day Bennington died), was "devastating" to Bennington. Both men battled drugs, alcohol, depression, and the pressures associated with being in a superstar band. "Chester and Chris were very, very close, and Chris's death was devastating to Chester."

podcast.title: Death Date Coincidence – 37 Years After Ian Curtis, Close to Chester Bennington
podcast.body: Cornell died by hanging on May 18, 2017 — exactly 37 years to the day that Joy Division singer Ian Curtis hanged himself. Two months later, on July 20, 2017 (which would have been Cornell's 53rd birthday), his close friend Chester Bennington of Linkin Park died by suicide, also by hanging. Cornell is interred at Hollywood Forever Cemetery in Los Angeles; his tombstone reads "Voice of our generation and an artist for all time." Johnny Ramone's monument is nearby. "Two months after Chris died, July 20, 2017, which would have been Chris' 53rd birthday, his close friend Chester Bennington of Linkin Park died by suicide."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death and End of Soundgarden Reunion
podcast.body: Chris Cornell's death in 2017 brought an end to Soundgarden's reunion, which had commenced in 2010. The band had successfully put aside a bad breakup from 1997 to record and perform for seven years, participating in a broader trend of bands reuniting due to changing music industry economics. "Soundgarden, a band that had a bad breakup in 1997, put all their differences aside in 2010 and continued to record and perform until Chris Cornell died in 2017."

podcast.body: After years as the singer for Soundgarden and Audioslave and releasing rock solo records, Chris Cornell decided he wanted to be a hip-hop star. podcast.title: Development of "Spoonman"
podcast.body: Chris Cornell took the name of a fictional band from the *Singles* movie, "Citizen Dick," and combined it with a musical snippet he wrote for an interstitial piece in the film. This creative process resulted in the song "Spoonman," which evolved from elements within the movie's production into a released track. "And after this movie, Chris Cornell took the name of that once fictional band, made it with what he wrote for that little interstitial piece and turned it into this."

podcast.title: Last Phone Call with Wife
podcast.body: During his last phone call with his wife, Vicki, Chris Cornell sounded groggy and slurred his words but assured her he was "fine" and "just tired." Shortly before the call, his bodyguard, Martin Kirsten, had helped him with his computer and given him two Ad-Avan tablets, a prescription for anxiety and insomnia. Vicki remained concerned after the call and asked Kirsten to check on him. "He sounded groggy and was slurring his voice, but said, no, I'm fine. I'm just tired."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lifelong Struggles with Mental Health, Drugs, and Alcohol
podcast.body: Cornell grew up as a loner, one of six children raised by a single mother who was an alcoholic; his estranged father was also an alcoholic. By age 12 he was drinking, smoking marijuana, and taking prescription medications. He tried PCP at 14 and suffered a very bad experience, deepening his depression and anxiety. He managed his mental health throughout Soundgarden's existence but after the band broke up in 1997 — coinciding with the failure of his first marriage — he went heavily into heroin and oxycodone. He entered rehab in 2002 and was entirely sober by 2005, except for prescription drugs. "No one really knows what one of the mill depression is. You'll think that someone has run of the mill depression and then the next thing you know, they're hanging from a rope."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins at Ray's Boathouse – Kitchen Work Led to Singing Career
podcast.body: In the early 1980s, long before Soundgarden existed, Cornell worked at a Seattle restaurant called Ray's Boathouse, starting as a teenager when his older brother Peter got him a job. He progressed from dishwasher to busboy to sous chef. At the restaurant's annual staff Christmas party, he spontaneously grabbed the microphone from a hired two-man band and launched into "Twist and Shout," astonishing everyone with the power of his voice. The bass player at Ray's Boathouse was Hiro Yamamoto; a maintenance worker named Scott Sundquist (later replaced by Matt Cameron) completed the original 1984 Soundgarden lineup with Kim Thayil on guitar. "Nobody had heard him before and nobody could believe the power of this kid's voice."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Period of Domesticity
podcast.body: Following his solo album and tour, and the soundtrack remix, Cornell entered a period focused on his personal life, settling down with his wife and having a baby. "Then there was a period of domesticity. Chris sit down with his wife, had a baby and just hung out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Death Lawsuits – Seven Demo Vocal Tracks, Royalties, Tribute Concert Proceeds
podcast.body: After Cornell's death, Vicki Cornell filed suits over two primary issues: the rights to seven vocal demo tracks recorded in early 2017 on his laptop, apparently destined for a new Soundgarden album, and the disbursement of Soundgarden royalties. Soundgarden counter-sued, alleging Vicki misappropriated proceeds from a 2019 tribute concert. Both sides went to war over social media rights and Chris's posthumous participation in any band activities. Vicki's offer of $4 million per remaining member, then $7 million, was refused. A settlement was announced on April 17, 2023: the seven songs will be finished and released. "This dispute has never been about money or the band. This is their life's work and their legacy."

podcast.title: Post-Soundgarden Break
podcast.body: After Soundgarden's sudden breakup, Cornell initially took some time off before commencing work on his solo record over 18 months. "The first thing he did was take a little time off."

podcast.title: Post-Soundgarden Solo Career Start – Free Agent
podcast.body: Following Soundgarden's official breakup on April 9, 1997, Chris Cornell became a free agent. He had a backlog of material and by 1998, he began working on his debut solo album, Euphoria Morning. "Soundgarden broke up on April 9th, 1997 with an official announcement, making Chris a free agent."

podcast.title: Roommate of Andrew Wood – Impact on Temple of the Dog
podcast.body: Chris Cornell shared an apartment with Andrew Wood, the singer of Mother Love Bone. Wood's unexpected death in March 1990 profoundly affected Cornell, leading him to write songs in tribute that eventually formed the basis of the Temple of the Dog project. "Andrew died the day Chris got back from a long tour with Soundgarden. A few days after the funeral, Chris and Soundgarden headed out on a European tour, and while on the road, Chris started running some songs in tribute to his old friend."

podcast.title: Wife's Concern and Remote Light Flickering
podcast.body: After his performance, Chris Cornell returned to room 1136 at the MGM Grand Hotel with his bodyguard, Martin Kirsten. Meanwhile, his wife, Vicki, in Los Angeles, noticed the lights in their home flickering on and off, controlled remotely by an app Cornell used. This unusual activity prompted her to call him at 11:35 PM, about 20 minutes after he left the stage. "Meanwhile, out in Los Angeles, Chris's wife, Vicki, noticed that the lights in the house were flicking on and off. Chris had an app that let him control the lights remotely."

xref.title: Formation (1984) – Early Lineup Changes
xref.body: Soundgarden officially started in 1984 with Chris Cornell, Hiro Yamamoto, and Kim Thayil, and an initial drummer Scott Sunquist. Sunquist was later replaced by Matt Cameron due to family commitments involving a wife and child. "In 1984, they started calling themselves Soundgarden with a German name Scott Sunquist. But he had a wife and child and couldn't commit to the band full time, so he was replaced by Matt Cameron."

xref.title: Andrew Wood's Death (March 19, 1990) – Heroin Overdose
xref.body: Andrew Wood, the popular singer of Mother Love Bone, died on Monday, March 19, 1990, the day before their album *Apple* was due for release. He was found comatose on March 16 after a heroin overdose, and after brain activity ceased, his family chose to take him off life support. "Andrew was a really popular guy, and he had lots of friends in Seattle. His death hit Chris Cornell, his old roommate particularly hard."

xref.body: The 1992 Lollapalooza tour featured the Jim Rose Circus sideshow, including Matt "the Tube" Crowley, who would swallow a seven-foot hose connected to a hand pump, force beer, ketchup, mustard, chocolate, and Pepto-Bismol into his stomach, then pump it all back out into glasses for audience members to drink. xref.body: The 1992 Lollapalooza tour featured the Jim Rose Circus sideshow, including performer Matt "the Tube" Crowley, who would pump beer, ketchup, chocolate, and Pepto-Bismol into his stomach via a seven-foot swallowed tube and then pump it back out as "bile beer" for audience members to drink. xref.title: Name Sold for $30,000 (October 2002) – To American Supergroup
xref.body: A group from Liverpool already named Audioslave was approached by the managers of the American supergroup (Chris Cornell with Rage Against the Machine's instrumentalists) to acquire their name. After initially rejecting a $5,000 offer, they were eventually paid $30,000 in late October 2002, just weeks before the American band's album release. "The managers rang them up and offered them $5,000 for their name. That seemed a little cheap, so they said no. And so the number went up and up and up. But since this was late October 2002, and the American AudioSlave album was set to be released in less than three weeks, the Liverpool AudioSlave knew they had the upper hand. In the end, they were paid $30,000 to go away."

xref.title: Post-Divorce Litigation (2003)
xref.body: After Chris Cornell and Susan Silver divorced in 2003, a lawsuit ensued. Chris sued for $1 million in damages, alleging that Silver, as Soundgarden's manager, diverted money owed to him to other band members. The suit also claimed she withheld his guitars, demos, journals, notes, and two Grammy Awards statues, and sought to permanently bar her from representing Soundgarden due to "irreconcilable conflicts of interest," which explained the delay in a Soundgarden reunion.

xref.title: Reunion and Subsequent End (2010-2017)
xref.body: Soundgarden, despite a "bad breakup" in 1997, put their differences aside in 2010 to reunite, record, and perform. Their reunion, part of a wider trend driven by declining CD sales and promoters' need for established acts, lasted until Chris Cornell's death in 2017. "Boomgarten, a band that had a bad breakup in 1997, put all their differences aside in 2010 and continued to record and perform until Chris Cornell died in 2017."

xref.title: Death (2017)
xref.body: Chester Bennington died by suicide via hanging before 9 a.m. Pacific time on Thursday, July 20, 2017. This date also marked Chris Cornell's 53rd birthday, with whom Bennington shared a very close bond. Cornell's death was "devastating" to Bennington, as both men battled drugs, alcohol, depression, and the pressures of being in a superstar band, ultimately described as "kindred spirits." "Chester Bennington died by his own hand, a hanging. One time before 9 a.m. Pacific time on Thursday, July 20th."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Death by Suicide (2017)
xref.body: Chester Bennington died on July 20, 2017, by hanging himself from a door in his bedroom, discovered by a housekeeper. The date of his death eerily coincided with what would have been Chris Cornell's 53rd birthday, suggesting a potential connection to Cornell's passing two months prior, which was described as breaking "something in Chester." Despite a vacation with his family in Arizona, Bennington returned to LA for an alleged Linkin Park video shoot, but "something went very wrong" that evening. No drugs or significant alcohol were found, and his autopsy revealed nothing of concern in his blood, leaving his motivations largely unknown. "The only possible clue is that July 20 would have been Chris Cornell's 53rd birthday."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Death by Suicide (July 20, 2017)
xref.body: On the morning of Thursday, July 20, 2017, at approximately 9 AM, a housekeeper found Chester Bennington hanging from a bedroom door at his house in Palos Verdes Estates. She alerted a driver who had arrived to pick him up for the TV commercial, and the driver subsequently called 911. "At around 9 a.m. on the morning of the 20th, a housekeeper found Chester hanging from a door in the bedroom."

xref.title: Final Performance with Chris Cornell (May 17, 2017)
xref.body: Soundgarden played a show at the Fox Theatre in Detroit on May 17, 2017. This performance would be Chris Cornell's last, and it elicited mixed reactions, with some observers noting that "something was off" with Cornell, while others felt the band was performing strongly. "On May 17, 2017, Soundgarden played a show at the Fox Theatre in Detroit. Depending on who you ask, the band was either on fire or that something was off."

xref.title: Impact of Chris Cornell's Death (2017)
xref.body: Chris Cornell's death in May 2017 deeply affected Chester Bennington, who attended Cornell's memorial service. Despite the difficulty, just days later, Bennington expressed feeling very creative, having written six new songs, and told friends, "we have to stick together, we have so much to live for." "But Chris Cornell's death really threw him for a loop. He attended Chris' memorial service, which was really hard."

xref.title: Audioslave Formed After Rick Rubin Suggested Chris Cornell; Be Real of Cypress Hill Also Auditioned
xref.body: After Zack de la Rocha quit Rage Against the Machine in 2000, the remaining three members tried to continue under the RATM name with a new singer. Be Real of Cypress Hill auditioned. But after some jamming, they decided they didn't want a Zack sound-alike — they wanted something new. Producer Rick Rubin suggested they talk to ex-Soundgarden singer Chris Cornell. The chemistry was immediate. They began writing as "Civilian" or "the Civilian project" but had to rename when they discovered another group was using that name. They chose Audioslave. The group was essentially Rage with a different singer, and they were productive from 2001 through 2007. "The chemistry was immediate."

xref.title: Black Calivados – Chris Cornell's Parisian Restaurant
xref.body: Chris Cornell invested in and owned a restaurant in Paris named Black Calivados, which he opened around the time he fell in love with publicist Vicki Cariannis, daughter of a New York restaurant executive. The restaurant is described as "very hip, very expensive," with decor designed by the individual responsible for Victoria's Secret fashion shows. The menu offers "New American" cuisine, featuring dishes like Caramelized Quail, Truffled Mac and Cheese, and Peanut Butter, Soul, and Popcorn Fois Gras, with a burger priced at approximately 40 euros. "But modeling is a fickle thing, so Chris decided to sink money into a restaurant in Paris called Black Calivados."

xref.title: Chris Cornell's Availability Post-Soundgarden
xref.body: After the dissolution of Soundgarden, Chris Cornell had not been actively involved in many projects. This made him available when producer Rick Rubin connected him with the instrumental members of Rage Against the Machine, leading to their collaboration and the formation of Audioslave. "Now Chris hadn't been doing very much since the dissolution of Soundgarden, so why not see if there was any chemistry there?"

xref.title: Chris Cornell's Initial Reaction to Jamming
xref.body: Chris Cornell arrived at the initial rehearsal with a "pretty cavalier attitude," expecting to know within 10 minutes if the collaboration would work. He realized it would be great almost immediately but stayed for an hour and a half before confirming his commitment to forming a band, despite the others wanting to continue jamming. They quickly developed seven songs within a couple of days. "Within 10 minutes, I knew that it would be great. But I stuck in there for maybe an hour and a half. And then they were ready to just keep going and keep going."

A guy named Kim Thale was brought in and eventually the Shims died out, but Chris, Kim and Hero started jamming together."

The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation as a Tribute
xref.body: Temple of the Dog was formed as a one-time-only band specifically as a tribute to Andrew Wood, who was Chris Cornell's roommate and a member of Mother Love Bone. "And as a tribute, he formed a one-time only band called Temple of the Dog."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation from Rage Against The Machine Members
xref.body: This band was formed when Chris Cornell joined the remaining three members of Rage Against The Machine (Tom Morello, Timmy, and Brad) after their singer Zack de la Rocha left. The group decided to change their name from Rage Against The Machine to Audioslave. "Tom Morello on the line. And I'm not really sure why there was a collective decision to jettison the Rage name in favor of Audio Slive, which is where we are today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation from Rage Against the Machine Remnants – Producer's Suggestion
xref.body: Audioslave formed when the remaining members of Rage Against the Machine (Tom Morello, Tim Commerford, Brad Wilk) sought a new singer after Zack de la Rocha's departure. Producer Rick Rubin suggested Chris Cornell, leading to an instant creative connection and the rapid composition of 21 songs. "Rage Against the Machine had imploded... All they needed to do was find a new singer... Then producer Rick Rubin suggested that they ring up Chris Cornell."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation of the Band
xref.body: After Zach de la Rocha left Rage Against the Machine, the remaining instrumentalists (Tom Morello, Brad Wilk, Timmy C) considered finding a new singer for Rage but were ultimately connected with Chris Cornell by producer Rick Rubin. During their first rehearsals, the immediate chemistry led to the writing of 21 songs in 19 days, including "Exploder," "Light My Way," and "Bring 'Em Back Alive." The members were committed to forming a full band, not just a one-off project, aiming for their new work to be "the best thing" they had ever done. "The first time we got together, we just jammed together and we decided, well, let's just try writing some songs. And I think the first three days of rehearsal with Chris, we wrote, exploder, light my way, and bring them back alive."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Friendship with Chris Cornell
xref.body: Chester shared a close and long-standing friendship with Chris Cornell. They toured together, socialized frequently, and Chester was the godfather to Chris's son, Christopher. Their bond was evident in their joint performances and mutual support. "Chester and Chris had a friendship that went back years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Initial Name Retention
xref.body: Initially, the new project with Chris Cornell was still intended to be called Rage Against the Machine. A bootleg CD with this title and featuring Chris Cornell exists, but Cornell's style diverged too much from the original Rage sound, prompting the band to reconsider the name. "In fact, I have a bootleg CD in my collection entitled Rage Against the Machine Feature in Chris Cornell."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

xref.title: Initiated Audioslave Formation
xref.body: After Zack de la Rocha's departure from Rage Against The Machine, Tom Morello contacted Chris Cornell to see if he would be interested in joining the remaining members of the band (Timmy and Brad). "On the other end was guitarist Tom Morello from Rage Against The Machine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Involvement with Chris's Foundation
xref.body: Toni is actively involved with Chris Cornell's foundation, which is dedicated to helping homeless, poor, and neglected children. "She's also part of Chris's foundation that works to help homeless, poor and neglected children."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Lane Staley's Death – Impact on Susan Silver
xref.body: The death of Alice in Chains singer Lane Staley was a significant event that occurred during Susan Silver's management tenure and personal relationship with Chris Cornell. This tragic loss was mentioned in the context of the difficulties Silver faced leading up to her divorce from Cornell. "Not to mention the total implosion and death of Allison Chains singer Lane Staley."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Lawsuit by Chris Cornell – Alleged Royalties Diversion and Withholding of Items
xref.body: Following their 2004 divorce, Chris Cornell sued Susan Silver for a million dollars, accusing her of diverting Soundgarden royalties to the other band members and withholding valuable items such as a guitar, Grammy Awards, demo tapes, personal recordings, diaries, and journals. The suit used strong terms like "fraud, oppression, and malice" in its documentation, and it was eventually settled. "Chris sued Susan for a million dollars, claiming that she diverted Soundgarden royalties away from him and to the other three band members, words like fraud, oppression, and malice reused in the documents."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Legal Fight Post-Chris Cornell's Death
xref.body: Following Chris Cornell's death in May 2017, the remaining members of Soundgarden entered into a prolonged legal dispute over the future of the band with Cornell's widow, Vicki Cornell. The band had been back together, recording and touring, seemingly settled into a new phase of their career before the tragedy. "And there's been a legal fight over the future of Soundgarden ever since."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 9: (20-11)

xref.title: Managed by Susan Silver and Kelly Curtis – Early Co-Management
xref.body: Alice in Chains was initially managed by Susan Silver, Chris Cornell's ex-wife, in partnership with Kelly Curtis. When Curtis shifted his focus to manage Pearl Jam, Silver took on sole management responsibilities for Alice in Chains, navigating the band through challenges including singer Lane Staley's death. "Kelly and his buddy Ken managed Allison Chains. When Mother Lovebone started to get hot, Kelly wanted to spend more time with them. Meanwhile, Ken wanted out, so Susan and Kelly became co-managers of Allison Chains through their own management company."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Members' Future Bands
xref.body: After the Temple of the Dog album was released, Chris Cornell and Matt Cameron were active in Soundgarden, while Stone Gossard, Jeff Ament, Mike McCready, and Eddie Vedder formed Pearl Jam. "By the time that Temple of Dog album came out, Chris Cornell and Matt Cameron were doing well in Soundgarden, while the other guys in the group stayed together in Formed Pearl Jam."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Nirvana Dissolution if Alive
xref.body: Speculation suggests that if Kurt had lived, Nirvana might have dissolved undramatically, with Kurt pursuing his non-grunge, acoustic musical ideas, similar to later unplugged shows by Eddie Vedder and Chris Cornell. "maybe he would just sort of dissolve Nirvana. Not a breakup, but just an undramatic fade to black."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Origin of "Spoonman" Name
xref.body: One of the alternative names Jeff Ament considered for the fictional band in *Singles* was a song named after "Artis," a street performer who played the spoons. This idea later contributed to Chris Cornell's development of the song "Spoonman." "But one of the other options was a song named after a street performer named Artis who played the Spoons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Personal Struggles and Fragile Nature
xref.body: Chester Bennington battled significant personal issues throughout his life, including childhood abuse, addiction to cocaine and methamphetamine, a drinking problem, persistent depression, multiple failed attempts at rehabilitation, and previous suicide attempts. He was described as having a "certain fragile nature," finding solace in his friendship with Chris Cornell, with whom he often shared his struggles. "He had all sorts of issues, abused as a child, addiction to coke and meth, a drinking problem, lingering depression, failed attempts at rehab, a couple of suicide attempts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 9: (20-11)

xref.title: Post-Grunge Evolution and Reunion
xref.body: Soundgarden sold millions of records during the height of grunge and later reunited, playing to sold-out arenas. Their journey eventually saw the tragic death of Chris Cornell, and the band subsequently broke up. "Sound Garden reunited and played to solo de Rinas and then Chris Cornell died."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Producers for Chris Cornell's Solo Album – Launchpad for Other Gigs
xref.body: The group Eleven, comprising Elaine Johannes and Natasha Schneider, played a crucial role in producing Chris Cornell's debut solo record, *Euphoria Morning*. Their work on this album garnered them further producing gigs for notable artists like No Doubt and Josh Homme's Desert Session projects, connecting them to members of A Perfect Circle, Nine Inch Nails, Danzig, Marilyn Manson's band, and PJ Harvey. "Chris reliant on both of them to help produce his debut solo record Euphoria Morning... who, based on this work, got producing gigs for no doubt in Josh Hommie in the early days of his desert session projects."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rage Against The Machine with Chris Cornell (Bootleg CD)

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rage Against the Machine with Chris Cornell
xref.body: Audioslave was essentially the remaining members of Rage Against the Machine (Tom Morello, Tim Commerford, Brad Wilk) with Chris Cornell as the new frontman, resulting in a significant musical "makeover" from their original sound. "Audio Slave, which, let's be honest, is really Rage Against the Machine with a big Chris Cornell makeover."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

xref.title: Reunion Delay – Linked to Lawsuit
xref.body: The legal dispute between Chris Cornell and his ex-wife and former manager, Susan Silver, regarding alleged diverted royalties and withheld band property, contributed to the delay in Soundgarden's reunion. This conflict involved claims of fraud, oppression, and malice. "So if you've ever wondered why it took so long for the Soundgarden reunion to come together, there's part of your answer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Reunion Post-Scream Album
xref.body: Soundgarden reunited the year after Chris Cornell's critically and commercially disastrous *Scream* album, despite previous expectations that a reunion would "never happen in our lifetime." "it'll never happen in our lifetime, Sound Garden reunion the following year."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Search for New Singer – Auditions and Rick Rubin's Role
xref.body: After Zack de la Rocha's departure, the remaining members of Rage Against the Machine auditioned several potential vocalists, including Be-Real of Cypress Hill, but none seemed to fit. Producer Rick Rubin eventually suggested Chris Cornell, which proved to be a pivotal recommendation, leading to the formation of Audioslave. "They auditioned a bunch of people, including Be Real of Cypress Hill, but nothing really worked. Then producer Rick Rubin suggested that they ring up Chris Cornell."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Susan Silver as Manager – Ex-Wife and Business Partner
xref.body: Susan Silver, Chris Cornell's ex-wife, served as the manager for Soundgarden. Her role as manager became a point of contention after their divorce in 2004 when Cornell sued her over alleged diverted royalties and disputed ownership of band-related items. "She is also the ex-manager of Soundgarden and Allison Chains."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Temple of the Dog (Undated) – Self-Titled Tribute Album

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Transformation into Pearl Jam – Post-Tragedy Rebirth
xref.body: Following the tragic death of Andrew Wood, the surviving members of Mother Love Bone, Jeff Ament and Stone Gossard, collaborated with Chris Cornell and Matt Cameron to form Temple of the Dog. This collaboration eventually led Ament and Gossard to form a new band with Eddie Vedder, initially called Mookie Blaylock, which soon became Pearl Jam. "When Mother Lovebone collapsed and turned into Pearl Jam, Kelly became their full-time manager, leaving Susan to deal with Allison Chains."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Transition to Audioslave
xref.body: After Chris Cornell joined the remaining members of Rage Against The Machine, they collectively decided to "jettison the Rage name" and reform as Audioslave. "And I'm not really sure why there was a collective decision to jettison the Rage name in favor of Audio Slive, which is where we are today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tribute Performance at Cornell's Funeral
xref.body: At Chris Cornell's funeral, Chester performed Leonard Cohen's "Hallelujah." He later tweeted about Cornell's voice, describing it as encapsulating joy, pain, anger, forgiveness, love, and heartache, and helping him understand these complexities within himself. "At the funeral, Chester sang Leonard Cohen's hallelujah, and he wrote this on his Twitter, your voice was joy and pain, anger and forgiveness, love and heartache all wrapped up into one."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tribute to Andrew Wood – Origin of the Project
xref.body: Temple of the Dog was formed as a quick tribute to Andrew Wood, Chris Cornell's former roommate and the singer of Mother Love Bone, who tragically died in March 1990. Cornell wrote several songs in his friend's honor, which he then shared with the surviving members of Mother Love Bone, leading to the formation of this supergroup. "When he got back to Seattle, he showed the surviving members of Mother Love Bone, the songs. When other materials started flowing, they decided to record a quick tribute album under the name Temple of the Dog."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Worked with Brendan O'Brien – Shared Producer with Chris Cornell
xref.body: Billy Talent is one of several prominent bands that have worked with producer Brendan O'Brien. O'Brien also produced Chris Cornell's 2015 solo album *Higher Truth*, demonstrating his wide-ranging influence across different rock genres. "he's a guy that's worked from everyone from Pearl Jam, to Billy Talent, to Bruce Springsteen, to ACDC."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Worked with Brendan O'Brien – Shared Producer with Chris Cornell
xref.body: Bruce Springsteen is among the acclaimed artists who have collaborated with producer Brendan O'Brien. O'Brien's production credits extend to Chris Cornell's 2015 solo album *Higher Truth*, illustrating his broad impact in the music industry. "he's a guy that's worked from everyone from Pearl Jam, to Billy Talent, to Bruce Springsteen, to ACDC."

xref.title: Worked with Brendan O'Brien – Shared Producer with Chris Cornell
xref.body: AC/DC has utilized the production talents of Brendan O'Brien, who also produced Chris Cornell's 2015 solo album *Higher Truth*. This connection highlights the producer's versatility and reach across various legendary rock acts. "he's a guy that's worked from everyone from Pearl Jam, to Billy Talent, to Bruce Springsteen, to ACDC."
